tldr: By introducing VLA-Feedback—a two-timescale architecture where heavy action chunk generation leaves only its final denoising step to be updated using real-time visual feedback—the authors dramatically boosted the success rate on dynamic tasks from 27.5% to 85.0%.
hero_caption: A comparison between conventional VLAs and the proposed VLA-Feedback. Conventional VLAs execute generated action chunks open-loop without looking at intervening frames, causing them to fail when targets move. In contrast, VLA-Feedback runs the heavy planner at a low frequency while a lightweight module inspects the latest image right before each execution step to correct the denoising direction, enabling real-time tracking.
overview:
While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at generalization, their massive size prevents running inference at typical control loop rates (e.g., tens of milliseconds). Action chunking—predicting multiple future action steps at once—is widely adopted to counter this, but it suffers from a fatal flaw: once generated, chunks are executed open-loop without adapting to evolving surroundings. In dynamic tasks such as catching a rolling can or dropping an object into a moving cup, the robot cannot compensate for discrepancies between planned trajectories and reality.

To solve this, the authors devised a clever mechanism that cleanly decouples heavy planning from high-speed feedback. In diffusion-based action generation, the process is deliberately paused right before the final denoising step, when the action trajectory is nearly complete. Then, at the very moment each action is executed, a lightweight module calculates only the final denoising velocity using the latest image from a wrist camera to correct the action. This allows real-time visual feedback to be incorporated in just a few milliseconds without rerunning the massive vision-language model.

Evaluated in simulation and on a physical Franka Emika Panda robot, VLA-Feedback maintained parity with existing methods on static tasks while boosting the average success rate on dynamic tasks from 27.5% to 85.0% in simulation, and from 51% to 73% on the real robot. It also demonstrated strong robustness to unseen velocities and visual appearances, presenting an elegant solution to the responsiveness bottleneck in action chunking.
contributions: Proposed VLA-Feedback, a two-timescale VLA architecture that repurposes the final denoising step of a diffusion model as a real-time feedback interface.

Achieved high responsiveness without disrupting the trajectory smoothness or action prior learned by the diffusion planner by applying corrections in the denoising velocity space rather than direct action-space residuals.
Introduced a two-phase training scheme that enables high-accuracy online corrections with only ~1.2M trainable parameters, without retraining the massive VLM-DiT planner at all.

Demonstrated through simulation and real-robot manipulation experiments that dynamic task success rates and robustness to unseen disturbances are substantially improved without compromising static task performance.

sections.heading: Missing Moving Targets: The Open-Loop Bottleneck in Massive VLAs
sections.summary: Although VLAs possess superior semantic understanding, high computational overhead and open-loop action chunking prevent them from adapting to dynamic environment changes. This paper proposes VLA-Feedback, which incorporates the latest observations into the final denoising step of a diffusion model, enabling per-step control corrections while preserving planner expressiveness.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that allow robots to follow natural language instructions have made remarkable progress. However, the vision-language models (VLMs) powering them are far too large to run inference at the high frequencies required for feedback control loops.

To bridge this latency gap, action chunking—predicting a multi-step future trajectory in a single forward pass—is widely used. While efficient because inference time is amortized over future execution time, execution is fundamentally open-loop. Incoming visual observations during chunk execution are completely ignored. Consequently, robots cannot react to cans rolling across a table or objects displaced by unexpected contacts made by the robot itself.

Prior attempts to address this have explored hierarchical setups separating thinking (low-frequency VLM inference) from acting (high-frequency lightweight action policies). However, using simple MLPs for the fast module reduces action expressiveness, whereas adopting expressive diffusion models increases latency and reintroduces the reliance on action chunking. Conditioning approaches like ControlNet also only incorporate observations at the single instant of chunk generation.

The core insight here is to embed real-time feedback directly into the denoising process of the incomplete action produced by the planner. The planner generates the action trajectory up to the penultimate step, and at each execution timestep, only the final denoising step is resolved using the latest wrist camera image. This enables real-time corrections at the control frequency while fully preserving the rich behavioral expressiveness of the planner.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of VLA-Feedback. (a) Conventional chunk-based VLAs swing and miss when a target moves mid-execution, whereas (b) VLA-Feedback updates actions on the fly using incoming images during execution, successfully catching moving toys.

sections.heading: Breaking the Expressiveness-Speed Trade-off: What Sets This Apart
sections.summary: While efficient VLA inference, diffusion trajectory generation, and dual-process (System 1/2) approaches have been explored, trade-offs between expressiveness and latency remain. VLA-Feedback is distinct because it neither trains a separate reactive policy nor adds post-hoc residuals, but instead uses the internal transition of a diffusion model as an update interface.
sections.details:
Prior efforts toward accelerated VLAs and feedback control broadly fall into three categories:

- **Efficient VLA Inference**: Techniques such as backbone pruning, token reduction, and asynchronous inference (thinking while acting) have been proposed. However, these either compromise model expressiveness, remain open-loop within chunks, or require complex mechanisms to smooth discontinuities across planning boundaries.
- **Diffusion-Based Action Generation**: Diffusion models and flow matching are exceptionally effective at modeling smooth, multimodal robot trajectories. However, iterative sampling incurs non-negligible latency, making it hard to inject new observations into an ongoing chunk.
- **Dual Systems (System 1 / System 2) and Feedback Correction**: Inspired by human dual-process theory, a low-frequency VLM (System 2) provides high-level guidance while a high-frequency low-level policy (System 1) outputs actions. Yet, making the high-frequency side expressive re-introduces latency, and directly adding simple action residuals via high-frequency decorators risks corrupting the natural trajectory prior learned by the planner.

In contrast, VLA-Feedback does not operate a separate, independent policy, nor does it tack on action-space residuals after the fact. Instead, it intervenes by correcting the denoising velocity vector on the near-complete action provided by the low-frequency planner. This precise integration point is the key to reconciling expressiveness with ultra-low latency.

sections.heading: Relinquishing the Final Step: Inside the Two-Timescale Architecture
sections.summary: Near-complete trajectory features generated by the low-frequency VLM-DiT planner are cached, and a high-frequency lightweight module fuses them with the latest image to predict the final denoising velocity. A two-phase training scheme with a frozen planner ensures both training stability and rapid responsiveness.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation: Feedback-Augmented Action Chunking
Language-conditioned manipulation is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). In standard action chunking, observation $o_t$ at planning step $t$ is mapped to a chunk of length $H$, which is executed open-loop over the next $H$ steps ignoring new observations. In contrast, this method uses a low-frequency planner to generate a penultimate action trajectory $\mathbf{a}^{k-1}_{t:t+H-1}$, and a lightweight feedback module $g(\cdot)$ refines each action into the final executed action $a^k_{t+h}$ using the latest observation $o_{t+h}$ at every execution step $t+h$.

### 3.2 Architecture Components
The system consists of two main pathways:
- **Planner Module (Low-Frequency)**: Built upon the GR00T foundation model. NVIDIA Eagle-2 encodes the language instruction and images into latent representation $z_t$, and a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) iteratively denoises the trajectory. Here, generation halts just before the final denoising step $k$, passing the near-complete trajectory $\mathbf{a}^{k-1}_{t:t+H-1}$ to the fast path.
- **Feedback Denoising Module (High-Frequency)**: This module features two branches for action and observation. Action trajectory features $\mathbf{e}^a$ are computed once during chunk generation and cached. At each control step $t+h$, the latest wrist-camera image is mapped to features $e^o_{t+h}$ via a lightweight encoder $\phi(\cdot)$. These are fused through cross-attention (a Transformer block) between action tokens and observation tokens, scaled by a learnable residual gate $\alpha$. Finally, a single-layer velocity head predicts the feedback denoising velocity $\hat{v}^{fb}_{t+h}$, producing the final execution action $a^k_{t+h}$ via a single Euler step (step size $\Delta k$).

### 3.3 Two-Phase Training and Inference Schedule
Training is completely decoupled into two phases.
In Phase 1, the entire planner is trained using the standard GR00T flow-matching objective (a regression loss between ground-truth expert velocities and predicted velocities).
In Phase 2, the pretrained planner is entirely frozen. Supervised regression is performed strictly on the lightweight parameters of the feedback module to match the ground-truth action $a_{t+h}^{\mathrm{gt}}$ using the planner's penultimate trajectory and cached features. This avoids backpropagating through the 3-billion-parameter model, making training extremely stable and compute-efficient. At test time, the system operates on a $1:16:16$ schedule: 1 planner call to 16 feedback updates and 16 action executions.

captions.F2: Detailed system architecture of VLA-Feedback. The low-frequency planner (VLM-DiT, left) generates a near-complete action trajectory and caches latent features. The high-frequency feedback module (right) ingests the latest observation at each control step, fuses it with cached features, and predicts the final-step denoising velocity to refine the action.

sections.heading: Never Missing Moving Targets: Overwhelming Performance in Simulation and Real-World Experiments
sections.summary: Maintaining baseline capability on the static LIBERO benchmark, VLA-Feedback increased simulation success rates on dynamic tasks from 27.5% to 85.0%, and on a real Panda robot from 51% to 73%. Latency profiling and ablations validate the benefits of fast visual feedback within the denoising space.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
For static tasks, standard LIBERO (Object and Goal) suites were used. For dynamic tasks, environments based on Robosuite were developed, including grasping a toy robot whose speed and direction change randomly every 2 seconds (1D/2D) and inserting a ball into a cup mounted on a moving cart. On a real Franka Emika Panda robot, evaluations spanned picking static bread, catching a rolling can, and placing a lemon into a cup pulled dynamically by a string. Baselines included OpenVLA, GR00T, and FiS-VLA.

### 4.2 Simulation Results and Reaction Latency
On static LIBERO tasks, VLA-Feedback matched the baseline GR00T (identical on Goal, a 2-point difference on Object).
The true advantage emerged on dynamic tasks. While GR00T reached an average success rate of only 27.5% (FiS-VLA achieved 40.8%, OpenVLA 2.5%), VLA-Feedback attained an impressive 85.0%. Even on "unseen dynamic variants" where object appearances, shapes, movement trajectories, and velocity ranges differed from training, it sustained a 78.1% success rate, confirming that trajectory corrections stem from runtime visual feedback rather than memorization.
In reaction latency analysis (time elapsed from obtaining a new observation to reflecting it in action), GR00T took 195.4 ms and FiS-VLA took 216.7 ms due to full-model inference. In contrast, VLA-Feedback achieved an expected latency of 18.7 ms thanks to its 2 ms feedback update.

### 4.3 Real-Robot Experiments
The physical robot trials mirrored simulation outcomes. On static bread picking, VLA-Feedback (90%) performed on par with or better than GR00T (80%). By contrast, on dynamic tasks like catching a rolling can (GR00T 35% → ours 65%) and placing into a moving cup (45% → 65%), the gap widened significantly, driving the real-world average success rate up from 51% to 73%.

### 4.4 Ablation Studies
Ablating components of the proposed architecture provided key insights:
- **Effect of Observations**: Removing the latest image caused dynamic task success rates to collapse.
- **Residual Prediction Space**: Replacing the denoising velocity prediction with direct action-space residual prediction (Direct Action Residual, $\Delta a$) severely degraded dynamic performance. While direct residuals on nearly completed actions are tiny and prone to unstable optimization, predicting denoising velocity vectors yields stable and appropriate corrections.
- **Feedback Frequency**: Decreasing feedback frequency relative to the planner (e.g., to 1:2 or 1:4) led to a steady drop in dynamic success, confirming the necessity of high-frequency intervention at every control step.

sections.heading: Not a Silver Bullet: Limitations of Local Corrections and Open Challenges
sections.summary: Because the method relies on local refinement at the final step, it cannot recover if the planner's initial trajectory is completely flawed or when disruptions are excessively abrupt. Enhancing robustness against wrist-camera occlusions and sensor noise in the real world also remains future work.
sections.details:
While VLA-Feedback is highly practical, the authors outline several clear limitations.

First, the approach is fundamentally a "local refinement." It assumes that the unfinished trajectory generated by the low-frequency planner lies within the neighborhood of a feasible solution. If the initial plan is fundamentally mistaken or an object teleports/moves drastically just before contact, a single-step denoising correction may physically lack the range to recover.

Second, real-world deployments introduce physical noise. Close-range occlusions of the wrist camera during grasping, actuator transmission and mechanical delays, and image noise can perturb small feedback updates.

Promising future avenues highlighted by the authors include adaptive triggering mechanisms that rerun the planner when plans become stale, as well as integrating predictive world models to compensate for observation delays and sensor noise.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A New Feedback Paradigm for Diffusion Models
sections.summary: By treating the final denoising step of a diffusion model as an interface, VLA-Feedback elegantly combines VLA expressiveness with real-time responsiveness. This design philosophy serves as a general framework applicable across all diffusion-based robot control.
sections.details:
This paper introduced VLA-Feedback, a two-timescale architecture addressing the open-loop execution bottleneck in action-chunking VLAs.

Rather than running the full VLM-DiT at every step or training a separate lightweight policy from scratch, the design smartly caches near-complete action representations and resolves only the final denoising step using the latest observation. This dramatically slashes latency to dynamic environmental changes without sacrificing dexterity in static tasks.

Using the terminal phase of a diffusion process as a high-frequency feedback interface is not limited to VLAs with language models; it directly generalizes to any robot control policy relying on diffusion models or flow matching for trajectory generation. It stands as an insightful milestone toward reactive real-world robot intelligence.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and the Secret of Lightweight Design
sections.summary: The feedback module consists of a pretrained ResNet-18 and a single-layer Transformer, comprising only ~1.19M trainable parameters. Freezing the planner during two-phase training drastically enhances training convergence and stability.
sections.details:
The appendix details architectural parameters and practical engineering choices during training.

### Feedback Module Specifications
The feedback module is engineered to be exceptionally compact. Its vision encoder uses an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 (~11.2M parameters, frozen) extracting 64 visual tokens. These are projected alongside action features into a 256-dimensional space and fused via a single-layer Pre-norm Transformer decoder with 4 attention heads and a feedforward dimension of 512. The residual gate $\alpha$ is initialized to 0.3, and a final velocity head ($256 \to 7$) outputs 7-DoF control commands.
While the total parameter count is ~12.4M, the vast majority belongs to the frozen ResNet-18; the trainable parameters amount to **only about 1.19M**. Compared to the ~3B parameters of the planner itself, this lightweight footprint is the source of its blazing 2 ms inference speed.

### Training Insights and Trials
Early in development, the authors attempted end-to-end joint training of the planner and feedback module. However, backpropagating gradients through the entire VLM-DiT was computationally prohibitive and frequently diverged. Switching to a two-phase strategy—freezing the converged planner and training solely the feedback module over the fixed action feature distribution—eliminated interference between long-horizon planning and local feedback correction, yielding remarkably stable training.

takeaways: When deploying massive generative models for action generation, instead of choosing between running the entire model or delegating completely to a separate small policy, an intermediate collaboration—running the bulk at low frequency and solving only the final step at high frequency—is remarkably effective.

While adding simple residuals in action space tends to destabilize training, applying corrections in the velocity field of diffusion or flow-matching models enables robust control without destroying natural trajectory priors.
High practical utility: dynamic responsiveness can be retrofitted onto an existing ~3B parameter pretrained VLA without fine-tuning it, requiring training of only ~1.2M lightweight parameters.
limitations: A single-step local denoising update has a bounded correction range (workspace limitation) if the planner's initial trajectory is completely off-target or if objects undergo extreme collisions or sudden jumps.
In real-world deployment, correction accuracy degrades when subjected to wrist-camera occlusions, actuator communication delays, or sensor noise.
The framework currently lacks an adaptive replanning mechanism to automatically re-trigger the low-frequency planner when an existing plan becomes completely stale.
